newsitem.title: USA: U.S. veterans want ban on depleted uranium weapons.
newsitem.headline: U.S. veterans want ban on depleted uranium weapons.

text.p: U.S. military veterans and former Attorney General Ramsey Clark called on Tuesday for a ban on depleted uranium weapons, saying the armour-piercing ordnance endangered soldiers in the Gulf War.
"It's absolutely essential that the use of depleted uranium in military (purposes) ... be completely banned," Clark said at a news conference.
Anti-nuclear activist and pediatrician Helen Caldicott, who also spoke at the news conference, likened the use of depleted uranium weapons to "scattering nuclear waste all over the earth."

Depleted uranium weapons were used during the 1991 Gulf War and the 1990 buildup for that war. When depleted of most of its radioactivity, uranium is a metal so hard that it is used to shield tanks and in anti-tank artillery shells.

The Defence Department did not immediately return a phone call on Tuesday, but Pentagon officials have previously discounted depleted uranium weapons as a cause of Gulf War syndrome, which can include chronic fatigue and multiple chemical sensitivity.

Sara Flounders of the Depleted Uranium Education Project, which represents veterans who blame various health problems on exposure to depleted uranium, said the substance's benefits as a weapon "made it enormously attractive regardless of what would be the human consequences."
The consequences for humans could include kidney problems, lung cancer, bone cancer and leukaemia, Caldicott said.
Gulf War U.S. Army veteran Carol Picou also suggested that birth defects found in the children of veterans were linked to exposure to depleted uranium.
Flounders called for an independent investigation into the effects of weapons and their link to disease.
